lead: A uniform beam's booms lose force from root to tip only because the bending moment falls. On a tapered beam the boom also slides inward as the depth shrinks, so its force changes for a second reason, and the inclined boom itself carries part of the transverse shear. The panel shear flow is then no longer S/h. That extra flow, the taper shear flow, decides how much shear a tapered spar web, a swept wing box or a tapering fuselage frame really carries.
prereq: You need: the boom-panel idealization from 5.6, the open-section shear flow rule from 5.2, and the bending stress M y/Ixx from Unit 4.

sections.h3: The boom force changes for two reasons

blocks.text: Idealize the section into booms that carry all the direct stress and thin panels that carry only shear (5.6). Boom i has area Ai and sits yi from the neutral axis. Its axial force is
P<sub>i</sub> = σ<sub>i</sub> A<sub>i</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> y<sub>i</sub> A<sub>i</sub> / I<sub>xx</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>i</sub> is the boom force in N, tension positive; M<sub>x</sub> is the bending moment at the section in N·mm; y<sub>i</sub> is the boom distance from the neutral axis in mm; A<sub>i</sub> is the boom area in mm²; I<sub>xx</sub> is the second moment of area of the idealized section in mm⁴.

blocks.text: On a uniform beam only M<sub>x</sub> varies with z, the distance along the span. On a tapered beam y<sub>i</sub> and I<sub>xx</sub> change with z too, so dP/dz picks up extra terms from dy<sub>i</sub>/dz and dI<sub>xx</sub>/dz (in the two-boom spar these combine into one geometry term). Taper angles stay small, a few degrees, so cos of the slope is taken as 1.
One rule covers both effects. Cut the section and list the booms the cut removes. The shear flow in the panel at the cut is

blocks.where: q is the shear flow at the cut in N/mm, positive in the direction of the cut; the sum runs over the booms removed by the cut; dP<sub>i</sub>/dz is the rate of change of boom force along the span in N/mm, and the minus sign means a boom that is losing force is handing that force to the panel.

blocks.text: This is the 5.2 integral written for booms. Freeze the geometry and it collapses to qb = −(Sx/Ixx)ΣAiyi, the ordinary bending flow. Whatever is left when the geometry moves is the taper flow.
Take a spar of two equal booms, area A each, a distance h(z) apart, with the midpoint midway between them so each boom sits at y = ±h/2. Then I<sub>xx</sub> = 2A(h/2)² = A h²/2.
Put that into the boom formula: P = M(h/2)A /(A h²/2) = M/h. The area cancels. The boom force depends only on the moment and the depth. Differentiate with respect to z:

blocks.where: M is the bending moment in N·mm; h is the boom spacing in mm; z runs along the span in mm; dM/dz = −S, where S is the magnitude of the shear force in N, taken positive when the moment falls outward; dh/dz is the taper slope, dimensionless and negative when the depth shrinks outward.

blocks.text: Split the two terms. The first is the flow a uniform spar of the same depth would have: q<sub>b</sub> = −(1/h)(dM/dz) = S/h, in N/mm. The second is the taper flow, at the same cut and the same sign convention:

blocks.where: q<sub>taper</sub> is the extra shear flow in N/mm; the total in the panel is q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>taper</sub>.

blocks.text: When the depth and the moment both fall toward the tip, dh/dz is negative, so q<sub>taper</sub> opposes q<sub>b</sub> and the web carries less than S/h. The reason is physical. The boom force acts along the inclined boom, so each boom contributes a transverse component P(dh/dz)/2. The two booms together carry P(dh/dz) of the applied shear and the web carries the rest.

sections.h3: Wings, swept boxes and the shear centre

blocks.text: A wing box tapers in depth from root to tip. For a linear taper dh/dz is the same at every station. q<sub>taper</sub> = M h′/h² is usually largest inboard because M is largest there, but the h² denominator also matters for a strong taper.

Sweep alone does something different. A swept boom's force Pi = M yiAi/Ixx depends only on the vertical distance yi, so a boom that leans only in plan has the same yi and the same dPi/dz; sweep adds nothing to q = −ΣdPi/dz. What sweep does add is a chordwise component P dx/dz of the boom force. That produces a chordwise circulation of shear flow round the box and a torque about the span axis, which moves the line of action of the resultant, so the shear centre of 5.1 must be read with care. The vertical taper term comes only from the change of depth with z.

In fact a strongly tapered beam has no fixed shear centre. q<sub>b</sub> scales with S, but q<sub>taper</sub> scales with M. The resultant position therefore depends on the ratio M/S at each station, which changes along the span and with the load case. A single shear centre is meaningful only when the taper term is small or happens to be proportional to S.

A tapering fuselage behaves the same way: stringers lean inward and their force has a transverse part. The examiner's check is always equilibrium: add the panel flows to the transverse boom components and match the applied shear force. Real sections that mix open flanges with closed cells are handled cell by cell in 5.8.

figure.caption: The bending moment sets the boom force; its gradient sets dP/dz and the bending flow. The boom slope turns part of the boom force into a transverse component that appears as a taper shear flow. In the worked example the taper term cancels 40 of the 100 N/mm bending flow.

spec.title: Taper shear flow in a two-boom spar

figure.aria: Block diagram: root bending moment gives shear force and a 200 kN boom force, the boom slope of -0.04 gives a taper shear flow of -40 N/mm, which is added to the 100 N/mm bending flow to give 60 N/mm in the web.

examples.question: A cantilever spar of 2 m span is idealized as two booms, each of area 250 mm². The boom spacing tapers linearly from 200 mm at the root to 120 mm at the tip. A tip load of 20 kN produces a root bending moment of 40 kN·m. Find the taper shear flow and the bending shear flow in the web at the root, and the total shear flow there.
steps: Span L = 2000 mm; h = 200 mm at the root, 120 mm at the tip. Taper slope dh/dz = (120 − 200)/2000 = −0.04, with z outward.
Boom force: P = σA = 800 × 250 = 200 000 N = 200 kN, the same as P = M/h = 40 × 10⁶/200.
Shear force at the root: S = 20 kN, the tip load.
Bending shear flow: q<sub>b</sub> = S/h = 20 000/200 = 100 N/mm.
Total: q = 100 − 40 = 60 N/mm in the web.
Full derivative check: dP/dz = (1/h)(dM/dz) − (M/h²)(dh/dz) = (−20 000)/200 − 1000 × (−0.04) = −60 N/mm, so q = −dP/dz = 60 N/mm.
Equilibrium check: web 60 × 200 = 12 kN; boom transverse components 2 × 200 000 × 0.02 = 8 kN; total 20 kN, matching the applied shear.
examples.answer: q<sub>b</sub> = 100 N/mm, q<sub>taper</sub> = −40 N/mm (magnitude 40 N/mm, opposing the bending flow), total web shear flow q = 60 N/mm at the root.
examples.check:
M = 40.0e6
S = 20.0e3
A = 250.0
h_root = 200.0
h_tip = 120.0
L = 2000.0
I = A*h_root**2/2
P = M/h_root
qb = S/h_root
dhdz = (h_tip - h_root)/L
qt = M*dhdz/h_root**2
qtot = qb + qt
dPdz = -S/h_root - M*dhdz/h_root**2
print(round(qb, 3))
print(round(qt, 3))
print(round(qtot, 3))
print(round(P, 3))
print(round(-dPdz, 3))

traps: Using only the local M and S and dropping the taper term. In the worked example that gives 100 N/mm where the true web flow is 60 N/mm.
Sign slip in dP/dz. Fix one positive z direction, measure dh/dz the same way, then confirm by transverse equilibrium of the booms.
Writing P = M y/I<sub>xx</sub> without the area. That is the stress in N/mm², not the boom force in N.
Mixing millimetres and metres in dh/dz. A depth change of 80 mm over 2 m is a slope of 0.04, not 40.
Quoting one shear centre for a heavily tapered beam. The taper flow scales with M, not S, so the resultant shifts between load cases.

quiz.q: State the shear flow rule at a cut in a tapered beam and define each symbol.
quiz.a: q = −Σ dP<sub>i</sub>/dz; q is the shear flow at the cut in N/mm, the sum covers the booms removed by the cut, P<sub>i</sub> is the boom force in N and z is distance along the span in mm.

quiz.q: Why does the taper term reduce the web shear flow when the section depth shrinks toward the tip?
quiz.a: The boom force acts along the inclined boom axis. Each boom contributes a transverse component P(dh/dz)/2, so the booms carry part of the applied shear and the web carries only the remainder.

quiz.q: A two-boom spar has boom area 300 mm² each, spacing 300 mm at a station where the spacing tapers at dh/dz = −0.04. The bending moment there is 60 kN·m and the shear force is 20 kN. Find q<sub>b</sub>, q<sub>taper</sub> and the total web shear flow.
Explain why a strongly tapered beam has no single shear centre.
quiz.a: q<sub>b</sub> is proportional to S but q<sub>taper</sub> is proportional to M. The resultant of the shear flows depends on M/S at the station, which varies along the span and with the load case, so no fixed point exists.

quiz.q: Give the boom force of a two-boom spar in terms of the bending moment and the boom spacing.
quiz.a: P = M/h for each boom, one in tension and one in compression, with M in N·mm and h in mm.

quiz.q: In the worked example the web carries 60 N/mm while S/h is 100 N/mm. Where does the missing 40 N/mm go?
quiz.a: Into the inclined booms. Their transverse components are 2 × 200 kN × 0.02 = 8 kN, and 8 kN spread over 200 mm is 40 N/mm of shear flow.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real wing boxes taper in depth and in plan at once, so a swept spar boom leans in two directions and production stress models keep the full three-dimensional boom direction. Finite element codes recover the taper term as a geometric contribution to boom stiffness. The same idea leads to shear lag in wide panels, to aeroelastic tailoring of composite wings (Unit 6), and to web sizing in light-aircraft spars.
